title: week 2 homework
introduction:
How technology has changed the way we watch
Before this class, I mainly learned about digital technology through computers, phones, apps and screens. I thought it was quite new, and closely connected with computers and coding. But this lesson on "the early history of digital technology" changed my idea. I began to know that many ways of thinking we see as digital today were already there long before computers came out.
The idea interested me most in this class is the difference between analogue and digital technology. We talked about how analogue has to do with being continuous, while digital means splitting things up into separate parts. 
This made me think about how we experience the world. For example, when we see someone walking, we see it as smooth, ongoing movement. But photography can split that movement into a series of distinct moments. The work of Muybridge and Marey shows how technology can be used to record and study motion. It make me see that technology does not just record what is real. It can also change how we understand it. Camera can take something we see as one continuous action and turn it into separate moments. When we put those moments together, we understand movement in a way our eyes alone cannot. From this, technology is not just a tool to record reality — it becomes a new way to see the world. Harold Edgerton’s work made me think more deeply about time. His high-speed photos capture very short moments that our eyes usually cannot see directly. A single photo lets us stop and look closely at something that happens far too fast.
This shows me that technology can give us different ways to experience time. It can freeze a moment, slow something down, or let us see things that happen too quickly for us to notice.
The Ninth Symphony is stretched out to 24 hours long. The process cuts the sound into very tiny pieces, then repeats and puts them together in new ways. I find this really interesting. It shows how technology can split sound into smaller parts and change how we experience time. A piece of music that once had a clear start, middle and end can become very slow and continuous like this. After thinking about these examples, I began to see a link between them. Movement, images and sound are all continuous experiences in themselves — but technology can break them into small parts. These parts can then be recorded, repeated, rearranged or changed.
This has helped me understand digital technology in a new way. It is not just about using computers. It is also about taking something apart and putting it back together in new ways.
This has also changed how I see my own work in Creative Technology. Before this class, I thought creating with technology was mostly about learning software, writing code, or building interactive websites. But now I see that technology is also a way to think about and question how we see and experience ordinary things. For example, I can film a common street scene, then split the video into separate still frames. I can take the sound apart, repeat certain moments, slow them down, or put them in a new order. The street itself stays the same — but technology lets us experience it in a whole different way.
The most important thing I learned from this class is: Digital technology did not start all at once when computers appeared. Some ways of thinking that belong to digital technology can be found in art and practice from much earlier times. Artists and inventors were already finding ways to break movement down, freeze time, study images, and reshape sound.
To me, this makes digital technology feel not like something totally new. Instead, it carries forward the ways people have always looked at, taken apart, and remade the world.
